t: Count Ways to Build Rooms in an Ant Colony — Linear Extensions as n!/Π(subtree sizes)
o: prevRoom encodes a tree rooted at room 0, and a build order is any permutation that starts with room 0 and lists every room after its parent — precisely a linear extension (topological order) of the ancestor constraints. Example 1 is a chain 0-1-2, so exactly one order exists. In Example 2, root children 1 and 2 root subtrees {1,3} and {2,4}; the two finished blocks interleave freely, giving C(4,2) = 6 orders, matching the listed sequences. With n up to 10^5, searching orders directly is impossible, but the count collapses into a product over subtree sizes evaluated modulo 10^9 + 7.
k: Valid build orders are exactly the linear extensions of the rooted tree, counted recursively by interleaving child-subtree orderings.
Appending an independently ordered block of size s behind t existing elements can interleave in C(t+s, s) ways; multiplying these factors across the whole tree telescopes to n! / Π sz(v).
Division modulo the prime 10^9 + 7 requires modular inverses via Fermat little theorem (pow(x, MOD-2)).

a.n: Approach 1: Bottom-Up Merge DP with Binomials
a.i: Compute ways(v): the number of valid internal orders of the subtree at v, combining its children left to right. After processing some children totaling t rooms, appending a child block of size s can interleave in C(t+s, s) positions, so ways(v) multiplies each child ways by that binomial. Precomputed factorials and inverse factorials make every binomial O(1); processing nodes in reverse BFS order removes recursion-depth risk for deep trees.
s: Build children adjacency lists from prevRoom and record a BFS order from room 0.
Precompute fact[i] and inv_fact[i] up to n modulo 10^9 + 7.
Process nodes in reverse BFS order; for node u merge children sequentially, multiplying ways(child) * C(total + sz(child), total).
Set sz(u) = merged total + 1 and store ways(u).

c.python:
class Solution:
    def waysToBuildRooms(self, prevRoom: List[int]) -> int:
        MOD = 10 ** 9 + 7
        n = len(prevRoom)
        children = [[] for _ in range(n)]
        for v in range(1, n):
            children[prevRoom[v]].append(v)
        order = [0]
        head = 0
        while head < len(order):
            u = order[head]
            head += 1
            order.extend(children[u])
        fact = [1] * (n + 1)
        for i in range(1, n + 1):
            fact[i] = fact[i - 1] * i % MOD
        inv_fact = [1] * (n + 1)
        inv_fact[n] = pow(fact[n], MOD - 2, MOD)
        for i in range(n, 0, -1):
            inv_fact[i - 1] = inv_fact[i] * i % MOD
        sz = [1] * n
        ways = [1] * n
        for u in reversed(order):
            total = 0
            res = 1
            for c in children[u]:
                res = res * ways[c] % MOD
                res = res * fact[sz[c] + total] % MOD
                res = res * inv_fact[sz[c]] % MOD * inv_fact[total] % MOD
                total += sz[c]
            ways[u] = res
            sz[u] = total + 1
        return ways[0]

a.t: O(n) — factorial tables are built once and each tree edge participates in one O(1) merge
a.sp: O(n) — children lists, BFS order, size/ways arrays, and factorial tables

a.i: Unrolling the merge recurrence shows every binomial factor cancels, leaving hook-length-style identity: the number of linear extensions of a rooted tree equals n! divided by the product of all subtree sizes. For Example 2 that is 120 / (5·2·2·1·1) = 6. One accumulation computes the sizes, then multiply n! by the modular inverse of each size. Same asymptotics as the DP but with far less bookkeeping.
s: Build children lists and a BFS order from room 0.
Accumulate subtree sizes by iterating nodes in reverse BFS order.
Multiply ans by pow(sz[v], MOD - 2) for every vertex v.
a.t: O(n log MOD) — one modular exponentiation per vertex; batch inversion brings it to O(n)
a.sp: O(n) — children lists, BFS order, and subtree-size array

w: Derive the closed form from the merge DP during explanation — interviewers reward seeing the telescoping. Pitfalls: recursion depth (trees can be paths of 10^5 nodes, so iterate in reverse BFS order); performing divisions without modular inverses; off-by-one in factorial bounds. Note room 0 contributes a factor of n! / ... like everyone else because its subtree is the whole tree. Follow-up: counting orders of a forest (same formula applied per component times interleaving binomials) or general DAGs, where counting linear extensions becomes #P-hard.
